script.opening: "Hello doctor, sorry to trouble you. It’s probably nothing to make a fuss about. I’ve coughed up a bit of blood — yesterday and again this morning, just a teaspoon or so into my handkerchief. Bright red. I’m not in a panic. I just… I suppose I wanted to know what it means, and what I’m meant to do if it happens again."

facts.text: Small volume: a teaspoon or two, bright red, three episodes in 24 hours. NOT a torrential or drowning bleed. Breathing currently no worse than his baseline. No chest pain, no fever, not light-headed. He is sitting up, talking in full sentences.
If gently explored: he looked it up. He found the words "massive haemoptysis" and "catastrophic bleed". The teaspoon frightened him less than the search results. He has not told Edith what he read.

HIDDEN AGENDA — under "what do I do if it happens again" is the question he cannot say plainly: "Is this how I die — am I going to drown in my own blood, and will Edith have to watch?" The fear is not the volume of THIS bleed; it is the manner of the death he now believes is coming.

Only if asked who’s with him and how she is: Edith is in the next room, "putting a brave face on". He is more frightened for her than for himself — the thing he most wants to prevent is her being alone with something terrifying and not knowing what to do.

Officially: to know what the blood means and what to do next time. Actually: honesty about whether a big bleed is likely, a concrete plan so that he and Edith are not helpless if it comes, and reassurance that he will not be left to suffer or to frighten her.

ice.ideas: "It’s probably nothing to fuss about" — spoken, but he’s read enough to fear it is the beginning of the end.
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — the manner of his death: that he will have a catastrophic, drowning bleed, and that Edith will witness it alone and helpless. The volume of today’s bleed is not the real concern; the imagined ending is.
ice.expectations: To understand what the blood means and what to do if it recurs. Underneath: honesty without abandonment, a crisis plan that protects Edith, and the promise he will not be left to suffer.

cues: "It’s probably nothing to make a fuss about" — minimising that invites you to minimise too; don’t take the bait, gently open it.
"What I’m meant to do if it happens again" — the request for a crisis plan; this is the clinical heart of the call.
A pause, or a question about whether bleeds "get bigger" — the drowning fear surfacing; name it kindly and answer it honestly.

checkpoints.text: Assesses the bleed properly and proportionately by phone: volume, frequency, colour, trajectory, breathing vs baseline, haemodynamic symptoms (light-headedness), and whether this is small-volume (current) vs a herald/massive bleed — without medicalising a dying man into a needless admission

Makes a proportionate management decision aligned with the agreed palliative ceiling of care and DNACPR: small-volume haemoptysis in advanced lung cancer is usually managed at home with the palliative team — NOT a reflex 999 call or suspected cancer pathway referral — while staying alert to reversible contributors (infection, anticoagulation)

Activates/strengthens anticipatory care: contacts or escalates to the community palliative team and district nurses TODAY; ensures anticipatory ("just-in-case") medicines and a crisis plan are in place; reviews any anticoagulation

Gives a concrete, usable crisis plan for a larger bleed: who to call (palliative line / DN, not necessarily 999), positioning, DARK towels/blankets to reduce the visual horror, crisis sedation (e.g. midazolam) available via the team, and that the aim is comfort, fast
Does not collude with "it’s nothing to fuss about" — gently opens the door to the real fear; names the drowning/manner-of-death dread when it surfaces

Answers the unspeakable question honestly and compassionately: a sudden large bleed is possible but not certain; if it happens it is usually fast; and — crucially — he and Edith will not be left without help or pain relief

Addresses Edith directly: that she will be told what to do, given the numbers to call, supported by the DN/palliative team, and not left alone and helpless — because protecting her is his actual priority

Closes with a held plan: palliative team contacted today with timescale, anticipatory meds + crisis instructions confirmed, exactly what to do and who to ring for any recurrence, a named follow-up call, and the explicit promise of comfort and non-abandonment

worked.txt: "You’re not troubling me at all, and I don’t think this is nothing — I think it’s frightening, and you’re being very calm about something that would unsettle anyone. Let me ask you a few practical things first, and then I want to answer the question I suspect is underneath the one you asked."

"A teaspoon or two, bright red, three times since yesterday — and your breathing right now, is it any worse than your usual? … No worse. Good. That tells me this is a small bleed, not an emergency this minute. Given everything we’ve agreed about keeping you comfortable at home, this is something we manage here, with your palliative team — not a blue-light trip to a corridor."

"You asked what to do if it happens again — and I wonder if part of you has been reading about this and frightening yourself. … You found the words ‘massive’ and ‘catastrophic’. Stanley, can I ask you the question you haven’t quite asked me? Are you frightened that this is how it ends — a big bleed — and that Edith will have to watch it alone?"

"Then here is the truth, because you’ve earned honesty, not fog. A larger bleed is possible — I won’t pretend it isn’t. It is not certain, and many people never have one. If it did happen, it is usually quick, and it would not be a long, drawn-out struggle. And this is the part that matters most: you would not be left to suffer it, and Edith would not be left helpless. We plan for it so that it is never the two of you, alone, not knowing what to do."

"So here’s what I’m putting in place today. Your palliative nurses will have medicine in the house — a sedative that works fast — so if a big bleed ever came, the priority is you being calm and comfortable within minutes. Practical things that genuinely help: dark towels by the bed, not white — it makes a frightening thing look far less so for Edith. One number to call, day or night — the palliative line, not 999. I’ll make sure Edith knows exactly what to do and that her job is to ring and to hold your hand, nothing more."

"I’m going to call your community palliative team straight after this and get the just-in-case medicines and the plan confirmed today, and the district nurse will visit. I’ll ring you this evening to check it’s all in place. You called to find out what to do — the answer is: nothing alone, ever. We’ve got both of you."

f.learning: Small-volume haemoptysis in known advanced lung cancer is not a suspected cancer pathway referral or a reflex 999 — it is a palliative crisis-planning consultation. Assess proportionately by phone (volume, trajectory, breathing vs baseline, haemodynamics), make a decision aligned with the agreed ceiling of care and DNACPR, screen for reversible contributors (infection, anticoagulation, low platelets; oral tranexamic acid or palliative radiotherapy discussed with the team), and then do the real work: activate the community palliative team and anticipatory medicines TODAY, and build a concrete crisis plan — one number to call (not 999), crisis sedation in the house (NICE NG31 anticipatory medicines), dark towels to reduce the visual horror, positioning on his side, someone staying with him, comfort-first. The hidden agenda is the manner of death: the drowning fear and, above it, the terror of Edith witnessing it alone. Decline the patient’s minimising, name the unspeakable question, answer it honestly (a big bleed is possible, not certain, usually fast, never unsupported), and protect the person he is most frightened for. Honesty without abandonment is the whole of it.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG31 (care of dying adults in the last days of life) · NICE NG142 (end of life care services) · Scottish Palliative Care Guidelines (bleeding; haemoptysis) · Resuscitation Council UK ReSPECT
knowledge.summary: Small-volume haemoptysis in advanced lung cancer is a planning consultation, not an emergency admission. Assess proportionately, treat what is reversible within his goals, and put a crisis plan and medicines in the house today.

points.t: Volume, frequency, colour, trend, breathing against his usual, light-headedness, fever or purulent sputum. A teaspoon or two with stable breathing is small-volume haemoptysis. Small bleeds can precede a larger one, so treat this as the prompt to prepare.

points.h: Decide within the agreed ceiling of care
points.t: DNACPR means no CPR; it does not mean no treatment. Ask what he wants if bleeding increases. Most people in his position want care at home, and the plan should say so and be shared with out-of-hours and the ambulance service (NICE NG142: coordinated care and shared records).

Chest infection, anticoagulants or antiplatelets (review and usually stop), and low platelets. Oral tranexamic acid is an option for haemoptysis (Scottish Palliative Care Guidelines; dose per BNF), and palliative radiotherapy can reduce bleeding — discuss with oncology or the palliative team.

NICE NG31: prescribe anticipatory medicines for people likely to need symptom control, with clear instructions. For bleeding, the crisis sedative is usually midazolam, prescribed by the team (dose per BNF). In a major bleed the patient is shut down peripherally, so a fast route (buccal, intramuscular or intravenous) is needed, not subcutaneous.

Scottish Palliative Care Guidelines: in a massive bleed, staying with the person and non-drug measures matter more than getting a sedative in; consciousness is usually lost quickly. Dark towels to absorb and hide blood, lie him on his side (bleeding side down if known), one number to ring, and someone present.

Many patients fear drowning and a loved one watching. The honest answer: a large bleed is possible but not certain; if it happens it is usually quick; he will not be left without help. Say it plainly.
Brief Edith directly: what to do, who to ring, that her job is to stay close. Offer a Care Act 2014 carer’s assessment and support afterwards.

dg.d: Open start; did not accept “probably nothing”; agreed to answer his actual question after the assessment.
Who is at home, Edith’s coping, what he has read, his wish to stay at home.
Proportionate phone assessment; district nurse visit today; no investigations that would not change care.
Tumour bleeding vs infection vs anticoagulant effect; small-volume vs herald of a larger bleed.
Screened breathing, dizziness, chest pain and fever; recognised that small bleeds can precede a major one.
Small-volume haemoptysis from known lung cancer, manageable at home, with a risk of a larger bleed.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Palliative team contacted today; crisis medicine in the house; dark towels, positioning, one number; tranexamic acid or radiotherapy discussed with the team.
Confirmed no anticoagulant; screened for infection; plan shared with out-of-hours and ambulance services.
Named triggers, the palliative line, a call at six this evening, and a conversation with Edith.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picked up the minimising, “what I’m meant to do if it happens again” and the internet search, and explored them.
Idea (nothing to fuss about, but maybe the beginning of the end), concern (a drowning bleed with Edith alone), expectation (a plan).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — the manner of his death: that he will have a catastrophic, drowning bleed, and that Edith will witness it alone and helpless. The volume of today’s bleed is not the real concern; the imagined ending is — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello Mr Pike, it’s Dr Lee from the surgery. Can I check I’m speaking to Stanley, and are you sitting somewhere comfortable to talk?
model.why: Identity and setting checks on the phone

model.text: Yes, it’s me. Sorry to trouble you. It’s probably nothing. I’ve coughed up a bit of blood, yesterday and again this morning, a teaspoon or so. I just wanted to know what it means and what I’m meant to do if it happens again.

You’re not troubling me, and I don’t think it’s nothing. You sound very calm about something that would unsettle anyone. I’d like to ask some practical questions first, then answer both of those questions properly. Is that all right?
model.why: Declines the minimising and sets an agenda that includes his questions

model.text: That’s fine.
Tell me about each time. How much was there, what did it look like, and has it been getting more or less?
Three times since yesterday. Bright red, a teaspoon, maybe two. Into my hanky. Not getting bigger, as far as I can tell.
And your breathing right now, is it any worse than your usual? Any dizziness, chest pain, fever, or changes in your phlegm?
model.why: Screens for haemodynamic compromise and infection

model.text: Breathing’s no worse than normal. No dizziness. No temperature. Phlegm’s the same, apart from the blood.
Are you taking any blood thinners, like aspirin, apixaban or anything similar?
No, nothing like that. Just the pain medicines the nurses sorted.
Thank you. That all tells me this is a small bleed and not an emergency this minute. Can I ask, who’s with you at home?
model.why: Proportionate interpretation and moves to context

model.text: Edith, my wife. She’s in the next room, putting a brave face on.
You asked what to do if it happens again. I wonder whether you’ve been reading about this and worrying about something bigger. Would it help to tell me what’s on your mind?
model.why: Opens the door to the hidden fear

model.text: I looked it up. It said massive haemoptysis, catastrophic bleed. The teaspoon doesn’t frighten me. That does.
Can I ask you the question you haven’t quite asked me? Are you frightened this is how it ends, with a big bleed, and that Edith would have to see it?
Yes. That’s it exactly. I don’t want her on her own with that.

Then I’ll be honest with you. A larger bleed is possible. It isn’t certain, and many people never have one. If it did happen, it is usually quick, not a long struggle. And the part that matters most: we plan for it now, so neither of you is ever alone with it, not knowing what to do.
model.why: Answers the question honestly and promises non-abandonment

model.text: Thank you. Nobody’s said it straight.

Because you’re comfortable at home and we’ve agreed that’s what you want, I don’t think you need to go into hospital today. We’ll manage this with your palliative team. There is a tablet that can help reduce small bleeds, and sometimes a short course of radiotherapy helps too. I’ll ask the team about both.
model.why: Management matched to his ceiling of care, with treatable options

model.text: I’d rather stay home. Definitely.

Here’s what I’ll put in place today. I’ll ring your palliative team straight after this, and the district nurse will visit. They’ll make sure there’s medicine in the house that calms you quickly if a big bleed ever came. Keep dark towels by the bed and your chair, not white ones. And one number, day or night: the palliative line, not 999.
model.why: Activates the team, anticipatory medicines and a concrete crisis plan

model.text: Dark towels. I wouldn’t have thought of that.

They make it far less frightening to see. If it happened, Edith’s job is simple: help you onto your side, stay with you, hold your hand, and ring the number. That’s all anyone would ask of her. Would you like me to speak to her too, now or this evening?
model.why: Addresses Edith directly and offers to include her

model.text: Could you? This evening. I’ll tell her we’ve spoken.
Of course. I’ll also update your plan on the record that out-of-hours doctors and the ambulance service can see, so anyone who comes knows you want to stay at home and be kept comfortable.
model.why: Shares the plan with out-of-hours and ambulance services

model.text: If the bleeding gets heavier, you get breathless, or you develop a fever, ring the palliative line or us straight away. I’ll ring you both at six this evening to check the nurse has been and the medicines are in the house. Can you tell me back what you’ll do if it happens again?
model.why: Specific safety-net, a dated follow-up call and teach-back

model.text: Dark towels, lie on my side, Edith stays with me and rings the palliative number. You’re ringing at six.
That’s it exactly. You rang to ask what to do. The answer is: nothing on your own. We’ve got you both.
model.why: Closes with a clear promise of support

model.text: Thank you, doctor. I feel steadier than I did.

social.t: Edith is coping outwardly and has not been told what he has read. Her readiness is part of his care. Ask how she is and involve her in the plan.
He wants to stay at home. Make sure equipment, district nurse visits and night support are in place, so a crisis does not become an admission by default.

legal.t: A DNACPR decision covers CPR only. Record his wider wishes (for example with ReSPECT) and share them with out-of-hours and ambulance services so they are followed at 3 am.
Attendance Allowance can be claimed under the special rules for end of life (SR1 form from a clinician). Edith is entitled to a carer’s assessment under the Care Act 2014.

professional.h: Honest conversations at the end of life
professional.t: GMC Treatment and care towards the end of life (2010): share information honestly and sensitively, and plan ahead for likely complications with the patient and those close to him.
NICE NG142: people approaching the end of life should have care coordinated across services and records shared. Handover to out-of-hours is part of the consultation.

community.t: Community palliative team and district nurses, local hospice at home, Marie Curie and Macmillan for night support, and carer support for Edith now and in bereavement.

redFlags: Increasing volume, clots, or a bleed larger than a few teaspoons — may herald a major bleed
Breathlessness worse than usual, dizziness or collapse — haemodynamic compromise
Fever or purulent sputum (infection); anticoagulant or antiplatelet use (reversible contributors)
psychosocial: Who is at home and how Edith is coping
What he has read and what he fears
His preferred place of care and death
ice: Idea: “It’s probably nothing to fuss about.”
Concern: a catastrophic bleed, drowning, and Edith alone and helpless
Expectation: to know what it means and what to do next time

playbook.diagnosis: Small-volume haemoptysis from known metastatic non-small-cell lung cancer, haemodynamically stable, no evidence of infection or anticoagulant effect; manage at home within his agreed ceiling of care, with a risk of a larger bleed that must be planned for.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “The cancer in your lung has a delicate surface, and small blood vessels there can leak. That’s what you’re seeing. It’s small now. We can’t promise it won’t get bigger, so we’re going to be ready.”

management.reflectIce: “Your worry isn’t really the teaspoon. It’s whether this ends with a big bleed and Edith on her own. Let’s make sure that never happens without help.”
management.psychosocial: Brief Edith directly and offer a call this evening; carer’s assessment; the plan on the shared record; hospice or night support if needed.
sharedPlan: Palliative team and district nurse today; crisis medicine prescribed and physically in the house (NICE NG31)
Dark towels, positioning on his side, one 24-hour number; tranexamic acid or palliative radiotherapy discussed with the team
Plan and wishes shared with out-of-hours and ambulance services (NICE NG142)
safetyNet: Ring the palliative line or surgery for heavier bleeding, breathlessness or fever
GP call at six this evening to confirm the visit and medicines; talk with Edith

pitfalls.intro: This station is not failed on haemoptysis knowledge. It is failed on two reflexes: sending a dying man to hospital, and answering the small question while missing the big one.

items.fail: “Call 999” or a same-day admission for a teaspoon of blood in a man with an agreed palliative plan.
items.why: “Management plan not appropriate for the patient’s circumstances.” It ignores his ceiling of care and his wish to stay home.
items.fix: Assess proportionately, then manage at home with the palliative team.

items.fail: No crisis plan: “ring us if it happens again.”
items.why: “Does not develop a safe management plan.” A major bleed at night needs medicine in the house and a plan the family can follow.
items.fix: Palliative team today, crisis medicine in the house, dark towels, positioning, one number.

items.why: Infection and anticoagulants are treatable even at the end of life.
items.fix: Ask about fever, sputum change and blood thinners; mention tranexamic acid and radiotherapy.

items.why: “Does not identify or respond to the patient’s cues.” His real question stays unanswered.
items.fix: “I don’t think it’s nothing. Can I ask what’s worrying you most?”

items.why: Protecting her is his main concern; ignoring her misses the point of the call.
items.fix: Tell him exactly what Edith would do, and offer to speak to her.

items.fail: Vague, soothing language: “let’s not worry about that now.”
items.why: Avoidance reads as abandonment and leaves the family unprepared.
items.fix: Honest, plain words: possible, not certain, usually quick, never alone.

timeMap.d: “It’s probably nothing” invites you to agree. Don’t. Promise to answer his real question after a quick assessment.
Volume, colour, trend, breathing against usual, dizziness, fever, anticoagulants. Decide: small bleed, not an emergency now.
Ask what he has read. Name the fear of a big bleed and Edith witnessing it.
Possible, not certain, usually quick, never alone. Palliative team today, crisis medicine in the house, dark towels, positioning, one number.
Triggers to ring, the shared record, a call this evening, a conversation with Edith, teach-back.

wordPics.fail: Sends him to hospital by reflex or reassures “it’s only a small amount”; never asks what he fears; no crisis plan; forgets Edith; or tells him “you’ll be fine” when he may not be.
wordPics.pass: Assesses the bleed sensibly; manages at home in line with his wishes; contacts the palliative team; talks about medicines and what to do if it recurs; basic safety-net.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: names the drowning fear and answers it honestly; a concrete crisis plan with dark towels, positioning and one number; checks for reversible causes; shares the plan with out-of-hours; includes Edith; a dated follow-up call and teach-back.

avoid.dont: “It’s only a teaspoon, I wouldn’t worry.”
avoid.instead: “It’s a small bleed, and it’s right that you called. Let’s plan properly for what might come next.”
avoid.why: Colluding with the minimising closes the door to his real fear.

avoid.dont: “If it happens again, call 999 straight away.”
avoid.instead: “Ring the palliative line, day or night. They know you and your wishes.”
avoid.why: A reflex 999 can mean an unwanted admission or resuscitation attempt, against his agreed plan.

avoid.instead: “A big bleed is possible, not certain. If it came, it would be quick, and you wouldn’t be alone.”

SCA_MODELS.text: Dark towels, lie on my side, Edith stays with me and rings the palliative number. You’re ringing at six.
That’s it exactly. You rang to ask what to do. The answer is: nothing on your own. We’ve got you both.
SCA_MODELS.why: Closes with a clear promise of support

SCA_MODELS.text: Thank you, doctor. I feel steadier than I did.

SCA_STEM.name: Stanley Pike
pmh: Metastatic non-small-cell lung cancer — best supportive care
meds: Symptom-control medicines as per palliative team letters
Anticoagulant or antiplatelet use: not clear from the record — to confirm
SCA_STEM.recent: Palliative oncology letter: no further anti-cancer treatment planned; best supportive care. No record on the GP system of just-in-case medicines being issued. Lives with his wife, Edith.
SCA_STEM.reason: Telephone call: has coughed up small amounts of bright-red blood three times since yesterday.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE NG31 (care of dying adults in the last days of life) · NICE NG142 (end of life care services) · Scottish Palliative Care Guidelines (bleeding; haemoptysis) · Resuscitation Council UK ReSPECT
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Small-volume haemoptysis in advanced lung cancer is a planning consultation, not an emergency admission. Assess proportionately, treat what is reversible within his goals, and put a crisis plan and medicines in the house today.

points.t: Volume, frequency, colour, trend, breathing against his usual, light-headedness, fever or purulent sputum. A teaspoon or two with stable breathing is small-volume haemoptysis. Small bleeds can precede a larger one, so treat this as the prompt to prepare.

points.h: Decide within the agreed ceiling of care
points.t: DNACPR means no CPR; it does not mean no treatment. Ask what he wants if bleeding increases. Most people in his position want care at home, and the plan should say so and be shared with out-of-hours and the ambulance service (NICE NG142: coordinated care and shared records).

Chest infection, anticoagulants or antiplatelets (review and usually stop), and low platelets. Oral tranexamic acid is an option for haemoptysis (Scottish Palliative Care Guidelines; dose per BNF), and palliative radiotherapy can reduce bleeding — discuss with oncology or the palliative team.

NICE NG31: prescribe anticipatory medicines for people likely to need symptom control, with clear instructions. For bleeding, the crisis sedative is usually midazolam, prescribed by the team (dose per BNF). In a major bleed the patient is shut down peripherally, so a fast route (buccal, intramuscular or intravenous) is needed, not subcutaneous.

Scottish Palliative Care Guidelines: in a massive bleed, staying with the person and non-drug measures matter more than getting a sedative in; consciousness is usually lost quickly. Dark towels to absorb and hide blood, lie him on his side (bleeding side down if known), one number to ring, and someone present.

Many patients fear drowning and a loved one watching. The honest answer: a large bleed is possible but not certain; if it happens it is usually quick; he will not be left without help. Say it plainly.
Brief Edith directly: what to do, who to ring, that her job is to stay close. Offer a Care Act 2014 carer’s assessment and support afterwards.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open start; did not accept “probably nothing”; agreed to answer his actual question after the assessment.
Who is at home, Edith’s coping, what he has read, his wish to stay at home.
Picked up the minimising, “what I’m meant to do if it happens again” and the internet search, and explored them.
Idea (nothing to fuss about, but maybe the beginning of the end), concern (a drowning bleed with Edith alone), expectation (a plan).
Proportionate phone assessment; district nurse visit today; no investigations that would not change care.
Tumour bleeding vs infection vs anticoagulant effect; small-volume vs herald of a larger bleed.
Screened breathing, dizziness, chest pain and fever; recognised that small bleeds can precede a major one.
Small-volume haemoptysis from known lung cancer, manageable at home, with a risk of a larger bleed.
Palliative team contacted today; crisis medicine in the house; dark towels, positioning, one number; tranexamic acid or radiotherapy discussed with the team.
Confirmed no anticoagulant; screened for infection; plan shared with out-of-hours and ambulance services.
Named triggers, the palliative line, a call at six this evening, and a conversation with Edith.

social.t: Edith is coping outwardly and has not been told what he has read. Her readiness is part of his care. Ask how she is and involve her in the plan.
He wants to stay at home. Make sure equipment, district nurse visits and night support are in place, so a crisis does not become an admission by default.

legal.t: A DNACPR decision covers CPR only. Record his wider wishes (for example with ReSPECT) and share them with out-of-hours and ambulance services so they are followed at 3 am.
Attendance Allowance can be claimed under the special rules for end of life (SR1 form from a clinician). Edith is entitled to a carer’s assessment under the Care Act 2014.

professional.h: Honest conversations at the end of life
professional.t: GMC Treatment and care towards the end of life (2010): share information honestly and sensitively, and plan ahead for likely complications with the patient and those close to him.
NICE NG142: people approaching the end of life should have care coordinated across services and records shared. Handover to out-of-hours is part of the consultation.

community.t: Community palliative team and district nurses, local hospice at home, Marie Curie and Macmillan for night support, and carer support for Edith now and in bereavement.

redFlags: Increasing volume, clots, or a bleed larger than a few teaspoons — may herald a major bleed
Breathlessness worse than usual, dizziness or collapse — haemodynamic compromise
Fever or purulent sputum (infection); anticoagulant or antiplatelet use (reversible contributors)
psychosocial: Who is at home and how Edith is coping
What he has read and what he fears
His preferred place of care and death
ice: Idea: “It’s probably nothing to fuss about.”
Concern: a catastrophic bleed, drowning, and Edith alone and helpless
Expectation: to know what it means and what to do next time

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Small-volume haemoptysis from known metastatic non-small-cell lung cancer, haemodynamically stable, no evidence of infection or anticoagulant effect; manage at home within his agreed ceiling of care, with a risk of a larger bleed that must be planned for.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “The cancer in your lung has a delicate surface, and small blood vessels there can leak. That’s what you’re seeing. It’s small now. We can’t promise it won’t get bigger, so we’re going to be ready.”

management.reflectIce: “Your worry isn’t really the teaspoon. It’s whether this ends with a big bleed and Edith on her own. Let’s make sure that never happens without help.”
management.psychosocial: Brief Edith directly and offer a call this evening; carer’s assessment; the plan on the shared record; hospice or night support if needed.
sharedPlan: Palliative team and district nurse today; crisis medicine prescribed and physically in the house (NICE NG31)
Dark towels, positioning on his side, one 24-hour number; tranexamic acid or palliative radiotherapy discussed with the team
Plan and wishes shared with out-of-hours and ambulance services (NICE NG142)
safetyNet: Ring the palliative line or surgery for heavier bleeding, breathlessness or fever
GP call at six this evening to confirm the visit and medicines; talk with Edith

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is not failed on haemoptysis knowledge. It is failed on two reflexes: sending a dying man to hospital, and answering the small question while missing the big one.

items.fail: “Call 999” or a same-day admission for a teaspoon of blood in a man with an agreed palliative plan.
items.why: “Management plan not appropriate for the patient’s circumstances.” It ignores his ceiling of care and his wish to stay home.
items.fix: Assess proportionately, then manage at home with the palliative team.

items.fail: No crisis plan: “ring us if it happens again.”
items.why: “Does not develop a safe management plan.” A major bleed at night needs medicine in the house and a plan the family can follow.
items.fix: Palliative team today, crisis medicine in the house, dark towels, positioning, one number.

items.why: Infection and anticoagulants are treatable even at the end of life.
items.fix: Ask about fever, sputum change and blood thinners; mention tranexamic acid and radiotherapy.

items.why: “Does not identify or respond to the patient’s cues.” His real question stays unanswered.
items.fix: “I don’t think it’s nothing. Can I ask what’s worrying you most?”

items.why: Protecting her is his main concern; ignoring her misses the point of the call.
items.fix: Tell him exactly what Edith would do, and offer to speak to her.

items.fail: Vague, soothing language: “let’s not worry about that now.”
items.why: Avoidance reads as abandonment and leaves the family unprepared.
items.fix: Honest, plain words: possible, not certain, usually quick, never alone.
